reference.source: ESC/ERS guidelines on pulmonary hypertension / Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
clinicalPearls: A rare form of pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension in which the obstruction lies predominantly in the pulmonary venules and small veins rather than the arteries
Presents like idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension with progressive exertional breathlessness, fatigue, and right heart failure, but is often more severe and rapidly progressive

Right heart catheterisation shows pre-capillary haemodynamics with a normal or near-normal pulmonary artery wedge pressure despite marked oedema, because the occlusion is downstream of the arterioles but upstream of the measured wedge
The characteristic high-resolution CT triad is smooth interlobular septal thickening (Kerley lines), centrilobular ground-glass opacity, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy
The diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide is typically strikingly reduced and hypoxaemia is often profound
Biallelic EIF2AK4 mutations underlie the heritable form and allow genetic confirmation without lung biopsy
Pulmonary vasodilators can precipitate acute, sometimes fatal, pulmonary oedema because the venous outflow is fixed while arterial inflow increases
Because response to medical therapy is poor, early referral for lung transplantation is essential
reference.pathophysiology: Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease is characterised by fibrotic obstruction and remodelling of the pulmonary venules and small veins, often with associated capillary proliferation. The heritable form is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in EIF2AK4. Because the primary obstruction lies in the post-capillary venous compartment while the arterioles remain relatively patent, pressure builds up in the pulmonary capillary bed, causing interstitial oedema, septal thickening, and capillary congestion, yet the pulmonary artery wedge pressure measured beyond the obstruction remains normal, so the haemodynamics appear pre-capillary. Administering arterial vasodilators increases flow into a bed that cannot drain, precipitating acute pulmonary oedema.
additionalDifferentials: Left heart failure with post-capillary pulmonary hypertension
Interstitial lung disease with secondary pulmonary hypertension
Mitral valve disease causing pulmonary venous congestion
additionalInvestigations: Right heart catheterisation demonstrating pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension with a normal wedge pressure
High-resolution CT to detect the septal-thickening, centrilobular ground-glass, and lymphadenopathy triad
Pulmonary function tests with a markedly reduced diffusing capacity
Genetic testing for EIF2AK4 mutations in suspected heritable disease
Echocardiography to assess right ventricular size and function
Ventilation-perfusion or CT pulmonary angiography to exclude chronic thromboembolic disease
redFlags: Acute pulmonary oedema after starting pulmonary vasodilator therapy
Severe hypoxaemia with a disproportionately low diffusing capacity
Syncope or signs of low cardiac output indicating advanced disease
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is poor and generally worse than idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension, with limited and hazardous response to medical therapy, so timely lung transplantation offers the best chance of survival.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension and initiating vasodilators that trigger pulmonary oedema
Attributing the septal-line and ground-glass changes to left heart failure despite a normal wedge pressure
Delaying transplant referral because of an apparent (but hazardous) initial vasodilator response
Overlooking the EIF2AK4 genetic clue in younger or familial cases
references: ESC/ERS guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary hypertension
Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
